title: Betting on movement
objectives: Build straddles and strangles that profit from a large move either way.
Find their break-evens and the risk of selling them.

screens.prose: A company reports results tomorrow. You expect a big move in its £100.00 share but cannot guess the direction. So you buy a call and a put, both struck at £100.00. The bold line is what the pair pays at expiry.
screens.question: The share ends at £88.00. What does the pair pay you?

hints.text: Which of the two would you exercise at £88.00?
The put lets you sell at £100.00.
The call pays 0. The put pays 100 − 88 = 12.

feedback.correct: The call is worthless and the put pays £12.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each option at £88.00, then add.

byKey.call-only: You looked only at the call. The put lets you sell at £100.00 a share worth £88.00.
byKey.loss: You treated the fall as a loss. The put gains £1.00 for every pound the share falls.
byKey.both: You paid out on both legs. The call is not exercised below £100.00.

explain.text: The call is left alone. The put sells at £100.00 a share worth £88.00, so it pays £12.00. One leg pays whichever way the share moves.

screens.prose: Slide the price at expiry across the whole range and watch the bold line. Its label shows what the pair pays.
screens.question: Where is the pair's payoff smallest?

options.text: At the ends of the range, where one leg is worthless
options.why: At every price one leg is worthless. The other pays more the further the share is from £100.00.
You followed the call's dashed line. Below £100.00 the put pays.

hints.text: Compare the payoff at £90.00, £100.00 and £110.00.
Look where the two dashed lines meet.

feedback.correct: The payoff is smallest at the strike, where neither leg pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to £100.00 and read the label.

explain.text: The payoff is the distance of the share from £100.00, in either direction. That distance is $|S_T - 100|$, a V with its point at the strike.

screens.prose: A call and a put with the same strike and expiry make a **long straddle**. The call cost £5.00 and the put cost £4.50.
screens.question: What does the straddle cost you in total?

widget.label: Total premium
widget.accept: £9.50: £5.00 for the call plus £4.50 for the put

hints.text: Did you buy or sell each option?
You bought both legs, so you paid both premiums.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You bought the call and the put, so add what you paid.

byKey.netted: You netted the premiums as in a spread. Here you buy both legs, so you pay both.
byKey.call: That is the call alone. You bought the put as well.
byKey.put: That is the put alone. You bought the call as well.

explain.text: You pay both premiums, £9.50 in all. The profit line is the V moved down by that amount.

screens.prose: Fill in the table leg by leg. Then take off the £9.50 you paid to get the profit.
screens.question: Complete the payoff table for the £100.00 straddle.

hints.text: At each price, only one leg can pay.
At the strike itself neither leg pays.
At £100.00 the payoff is 0, so the profit is 0 − 9.50 = −9.50.

feedback.correct: A £15.00 move either way makes £5.50; no move loses £9.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each leg, add them, then take off £9.50.

byKey.r0c2: At £85.00 the put sells at £100.00 a share worth £85.00.
byKey.r1c4: The put pays £5.00, which does not cover the £9.50 cost.
byKey.r2c4: At the strike neither leg pays, so you lose both premiums.
byKey.r3c4: The call pays £15.00. Take off the £9.50 you paid.

explain.text: At £100.00 both legs expire worthless and you lose the full £9.50, the worst case. A £15.00 move either way gives the same £5.50. The profit line is symmetric about the strike.

screens.prose: The straddle makes money only once the move has paid back both premiums. The break-even markers are hidden.
screens.question: Find the two break-even prices.

hints.text: How far must the share move to pay back £9.50?
Below the strike the put pays $100 - S_T$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each side has to recover both premiums.

byKey.r0c1: Below the strike the put must pay back all £9.50: $100 - S_T = 9.50$.
byKey.r1c1: Above the strike the call must pay back all £9.50: $S_T - 100 = 9.50$.

explain.text: Each side must recover both premiums. So the break-evens are $100 \pm 9.50$: £90.50 and £109.50. Between them the straddle loses money.

screens.prose: A friend says a straddle cannot lose: whichever way the share goes, one leg pays. The share ends at £104.00. The diagram shows the payoff, before premiums.
screens.question: What is the straddle's profit at £104.00?

options.why: You took the call's payoff and forgot the £9.50 you paid for both legs.
You assumed a straddle cannot lose. One leg pays, but only £4.00 against a £9.50 cost.
You took off only the call's £5.00 premium. You paid for the put too.

hints.text: What did the two legs cost together?
At £104.00 the call pays £4.00 and the put nothing.
Profit is 4.00 − 9.50.

feedback.correct: The call pays £4.00, but you paid £9.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the cost of both legs off the payoff.

byKey.b: That is the payoff, not the profit. You paid £9.50 for the pair.
byKey.c: One leg always pays, but it can pay less than the pair cost.

explain.text: The call pays £4.00 and the put nothing. You paid £9.50, so the profit is $4 - 9.50 = -5.50$. A straddle loses whenever the move is smaller than the premiums.

screens.prose: Move the strikes apart. Buy a put struck at £95.00 for £2.20 and a call struck at £105.00 for £2.80. This is a **long strangle**. Slide the price to explore it.
screens.question: Fill in the strangle's cost and break-evens.

hints.text: You bought both legs, so add the premiums.
Below £95.00 the put pays $95 - S_T$; above £105.00 the call pays $S_T - 105$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the premiums, then measure from each strike.

byKey.r1c1: The put must pay back £5.00, starting from its own strike, £95.00.
byKey.r2c1: The call must pay back £5.00, starting from its own strike, £105.00.

explain.text: The strangle costs £5.00, about half the straddle. But it pays nothing between £95.00 and £105.00. Its break-evens, £90.00 and £110.00, need a bigger move than the straddle's £90.50 and £109.50.

screens.prose: Now sell the straddle: you write the call and the put. You collect £9.50 and hope the share stays calm. This is a **short straddle**.
screens.question: The share jumps to £130.00. What is your profit?

widget.label: Profit of the short straddle
widget.accept: −£20.50: £9.50 collected less £30.00 owed on the call

hints.text: Which leg is exercised against you at £130.00?
The call's buyer buys from you at £100.00 a share worth £130.00.
You owe £30.00 and collected £9.50: 9.50 − 30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take what you owe on the call off the premiums you collected.

byKey.nopremium: You forgot the £9.50 you collected at the start.
byKey.best: That is your best case, at £100.00. At £130.00 the call is exercised against you.
byKey.buyer: That is the buyer's profit. As the seller you have the opposite sign.

explain.text: The call you wrote costs you £30.00, and the premiums cushion only £9.50. The seller's best case is £9.50 at the strike. The loss keeps growing as the share moves further.

screens.prose: You found the payoff as the distance from the strike. With total premium $c + p$: $$\text{profit} = |S_T - K| - (c + p).$$ The break-evens are $K \pm (c + p)$. The worst case is $S_T = K$, which loses $c + p$.
screens.question: A straddle struck at £80.00 costs £6.00 in total. Where are its break-evens?

options.why: That is the strike, the worst point, where you lose the full £6.00.
You split the £6.00 between the two sides. Each side must recover all of it.
You checked the call side alone. The put side breaks even too, at £74.00.

explain.text: Each side must recover the whole £6.00. Below the strike that happens at £74.00, above it at £86.00.

screens.prose: A share at £100.00 reports results tomorrow, and the options expire just after. A week ago this straddle cost £6.00. Today it costs £9.50: traders expect a big move, so **implied volatility** has risen. On past results days the share moved £8.00 on average.
screens.question: The share moves £8.00, either way. What is your profit if you buy the straddle today?

hints.text: An £8.00 move either way gives the same payoff.
Today's price is £9.50, not last week's £6.00.
Profit is 8.00 − 9.50.

feedback.correct: The move pays £8.00 against a £9.50 cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take today's price off the £8.00 payoff.

byKey.nocost: That is the payoff. You paid £9.50 for it.
byKey.lastweek: That uses last week's £6.00. The price has risen since.
byKey.onepremium: You took off only the call's £5.00. You pay for the put too.
byKey.sign: The £8.00 payoff against a £9.50 cost is 8 − 9.5, which is below zero. A positive £1.50 takes 9.5 − 8, the wrong way round.

explain.text: An £8.00 move pays £8.00 against a £9.50 cost, a loss of £1.50. Bought last week at £6.00, the same move would have made £2.00. Before results, straddles are dear because the expected move is already in the price.

ideas: A long straddle is a call and a put at the same strike. Its payoff is $|S_T - K|$, whichever way the share moves.
It profits only once the move passes both premiums: the break-evens are $K \pm (c + p)$.
A strangle with strikes apart is cheaper but needs a bigger move. Selling either is a bet on calm, with large losses on a big move.

formula.name: Long straddle profit
formula.note: Worst case at $S_T = K$: you lose both premiums.

summary.trap: One leg always pays, but a straddle still loses when the move is smaller than the two premiums together.

quiz.prose: You bought the £100.00 straddle for £9.50. The share ends at exactly £100.00.
quiz.question: What is your profit?

feedback.correct: Neither leg pays, so you lose both premiums.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the payoff at the strike, then take off the cost.

byKey.payoff: That is the payoff. You paid £9.50 for it.
byKey.half: You lost both premiums, not half of them.
byKey.sign: That is the seller's profit, not yours.

explain.text: At $S_T = K$ the call and the put are both worthless. You lose the whole £9.50, the straddle's worst case.

quiz.prose: A straddle struck at £50.00: the call costs £3.00 and the put £2.50.
quiz.question: Where is its upper break-even?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The call side must recover the cost of both legs.

byKey.callonly: You recovered only the call's £3.00. The put cost £2.50 too.
byKey.strike: That is the strike, where you lose the most.
byKey.half: You split the cost between the two sides. Each side must recover all of it.

explain.text: The total premium is $3.00 + 2.50 = 5.50$. Above the strike the call must pay that back, at $50 + 5.50 = 55.50$.

quiz.prose: Compare the £100.00 straddle at £9.50 with the £95.00/£105.00 strangle at £5.00.
quiz.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The strangle is cheaper but needs a bigger move to break even
The strangle is cheaper and breaks even sooner
options.why: Cheaper, yes. But its strikes sit £5.00 from the centre, so its break-evens are £90.00 and £110.00.

options.text: The strangle costs more because it has two strikes
options.why: Both have two legs. Out-of-the-money options cost less, so the strangle is cheaper.

options.text: They break even at the same prices
options.why: The straddle breaks even at £90.50 and £109.50, the strangle at £90.00 and £110.00.

feedback.correct: Half the cost, but break-evens further out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the costs, then the break-evens.

explain.text: The strangle's break-evens are $95 - 5 = 90$ and $105 + 5 = 110$. The straddle's are £90.50 and £109.50. The cheaper bet needs a wider move.

quiz.prose: You sell the £100.00 straddle and collect £9.50.
quiz.question: For which expiry prices do you make money?

options.text: At any price, because you keep the premium
options.why: You keep the £9.50, but you owe the payoff. A big move costs more than £9.50.
That is where the buyer makes money. The seller wins in the middle.
£100.00 is your best price, but nearby prices still leave part of the £9.50.

feedback.correct: The seller wins whenever the move is smaller than £9.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The seller's profit is the buyer's, with the sign flipped.

explain.text: The seller's profit is $9.50 - |S_T - 100|$. It is positive while the share stays within £9.50 of the strike.
